mainEntity.name: Why does Excel give a different Q1 than my textbook?

acceptedAnswer.text: Excel’s QUARTILE.INC interpolates at rank 1 + 0.25(n − 1), while many textbooks take the median of the lower half. Both are legitimate definitions; the comparison table above shows the results side by side for your data.

mainEntity.name: What is the interquartile range used for?

acceptedAnswer.text: It measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data and, unlike the range or standard deviation, is barely affected by extreme values. It is also the basis of Tukey’s outlier fences.

mainEntity.name: How are mild and extreme outliers classified?

acceptedAnswer.text: A value beyond 1.5 × IQR from the nearer quartile is a mild outlier; beyond 3 × IQR it is an extreme outlier. The 1.5 and 3 multipliers are Tukey’s conventions rather than laws of nature.

mainEntity.name: Can the lower fence be negative when all data is positive?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The fence is a calculation from Q1 and the IQR, so it can fall below zero even if every value is positive. It simply means no value is low enough to be flagged at the bottom.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between quartiles and percentiles?

acceptedAnswer.text: Quartiles are specific percentiles: Q1 is the 25th, Q2 the 50th and Q3 the 75th. Percentile methods share the same definitional choices as the quartile methods on this page.

mainEntity.name: How many values do I need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Quartiles can be computed from as few as two values with the inclusive and hinge methods, but they are only meaningful with a reasonable amount of data. The exclusive method requires at least three values.
